name: Evaluation Datasets
blurb: Benchmarks and test sets, and what each actually measures.

items.note: Grade-school math word problems; the standard arithmetic-reasoning test
Science exam questions in easy and challenge splits
57-subject knowledge exam; the most-cited general capability benchmark
The successor suite to GLUE for language understanding
Commonsense sentence completion designed to be adversarial to models
164 hand-written programming problems; the original code-generation benchmark
The harder ten-choice successor as frontier models saturated MMLU
Graduate-level science questions that resist search; gated to keep answers out of training data

reading.body:
Evaluation datasets are becoming harder and more specialized as frontier models saturate the benchmarks designed to measure them. The nine most-used evaluation datasets span arithmetic, science knowledge, language understanding, code generation, and instruction-following, with download counts ranging from 1.2 million for grade-school math down to 121,000 for graduate-level science questions. GSM8K, AI2 ARC, and MMLU dominate by usage, but MMLU-Pro exists explicitly because frontier models have exhausted the original MMLU's signal. This pattern shows the benchmark-saturation cycle: a test becomes standard, models converge toward it, researchers design a harder successor.

This matters for AI capability claims because benchmarks measure narrow slices of capability and change as models improve. A model that tops MMLU does not necessarily understand science; MMLU measures recognition across 57 subjects at introductory depth. The shift to MMLU-Pro, harder science questions, and adversarial commonsense tests suggests that older benchmarks are no longer discriminating between capable and less capable models. This does not mean frontier models have plateaued in absolute capability, only that the evaluation tools no longer distinguish performance differences at the frontier.

What these datasets do not capture is the relationship between capability and the resources required to produce it. They measure what a model knows or can do, not how much compute, power, or physical infrastructure was needed to train it. A benchmark cannot tell you whether a harder result required proportionally more data, compute, or electricity. The datasets themselves are small relative to training corpora. They also remain largely academic, designed by universities and research labs, not by the infrastructure operators who will ultimately constrain AI scaling.
